content:

John ‘Pinocchio’ Henty’s case ends in acquittal

A court case brought by former Essex & Suffolk Hunt huntsman John Henty against a hunt saboteur has ended in a resounding victory for the defence, with the saboteur found NOT GUILTY.




John Henty outside court.




Following allegations made to police, former Essex & Suffolk Hunt huntsman John Henty pursued a prosecution alleging abusive and threatening behaviour under Section 5 of the Public Order Act. The case followed an incident on a quiet country lane in which Henty pursued the hunt saboteurs’ vehicle, blocked it in, approached it and attempted to provoke a reaction.




What followed was a lengthy legal process based on Henty’s account of events. However, when his evidence was examined in court, serious questions arose about the credibility of that account and whether the alleged behaviour actually amounted to a criminal offence.




A case that should never have reached court?




The Judge was highly critical of the way the case had been handled by the CPS and the police officers involved, making clear that the alleged actions did not meet the legal threshold required for a criminal offence.

title: No Land, No Hunting
content:
Thank you to West Midlands Hunt Saboteurs for this guest article.




On Thursday 8th October, West Midlands Hunt Sabs (WMHS) held a protest outside The Bower House in Shipston on Stour. The restaurant is owned by Andrew Stephen Bower Knight, who continually allows, not only the Warwickshire Hunt to illegally hunt foxes on his land at Compton Scorpion, but the North Cotswold Hunt too.




The protest caused quite a stir amongst the pro-hunt community prompting the British Hound Sports Association (BHSA) to publish a social media post stating 

“Rural businesses are under attack by urban saboteurs.”




Visitors to The Bower House in Shipston on Stour were made aware that business owner, Andrew Stephen Bower Knight, enables illegal fox hunting.




The campaign against the Warwickshire Hunt is one that spans back years and is steeped in controversy, including the fact that Warwickshire Police entered into a “secret deal” with the hunt when they withdrew the Community Protection Notice that they had been issued.




WMHS have always highlighted the importance of holding landowners to account, something which featured heavily in the campaign against the now defunct Atherstone Hunt. The Hunting Act stipulates that should a landowner allow the hunting of a wild mammal with dogs on their land then they are breaking the law.

title: Smokescreen Saturday Exposed: Chris Packham Blasts The Quorn Hunt Over Sickening Fox Cruelty That Blows Apart Trail Hunting’s Biggest Lie
content:
When we showed wildlife campaigner Chris Packham the sickening footage of the Quorn Hunt, his response was damning:




“Another bloody year, another bloodied body, another animal tortured and torn to pieces to gratify the bloodlust of savages. Where is the damned consultation and where is the damned ban?”




Chris Packham condemns the Quorn Hunt footage.




The footage lays bare the brutal reality of cub hunting – the practice of using foxes to train young hounds to hunt and kill.




WARNING: DISTURBING FOOTAGE










Cub hunting is not some isolated activity. It is the preparation for the hunting season ahead. Throughout the autumn, young hounds are taught what to chase, what to kill and how to respond to the huntsman’s commands. What they learn – or fail to learn – during these crucial weeks sets the tone for the entire season.




This is what makes the Quorn Hunt footage so damning. It shows hounds being deliberately encouraged to seize and tear at a fox, with hunt staff repeatedly intervening to reinforce that behaviour.




On the eve of National Trail Hunting Day aka Smokescreen Saturday – as the British Hound Sports Association (BHSA) and the Countryside Alliance prepared to showcase so-called ‘trail hunting’, the Quorn Hunt provided a horrifying glimpse of the reality behind the myth of trail laying.

author: webadmin
title: All Warning, No Action?
content:
As more hunts receive police warnings and notices, are they a route to meaningful action, or a substitute for it?




Many of you cannot have failed to notice that we are writing more and more about hunts being issued with Community Protection Warnings (CPWs) and, occasionally, the CPW’s big sister, the Community Protection Notice (CPN). The former of course precedes the latter.




What in the puck is this? The Puckeridge and Essex Hunts have had 3 CPWs and a CPN and they still ignore them. Image: East Herts Hunt Sabs.




The Community Protection Notice system, including the requirement to issue a warning first, was introduced in 2014 by David Cameron’s Conservative-led coalition government, under then Home Secretary Theresa May as part of the Anti-social Behaviour, Crime & Policing Act 2014.




The irony that these measures are now being used, more and more, to regulate the conduct of fox hunts, an activity that has recently been publicly defended by Cameron, is not lost on us.




A CPW is not a criminal conviction. Ignoring one is not, in itself, a criminal offence, and there is no automatic penalty for failing to comply. If the behaviour continues, the police can escalate matters by issuing a CPN. Unlike a warning, a CPN imposes legally enforceable requirements, and breaching those requirements without reasonable excuse is a criminal offence.
